 Thanksgiving deserves more than a passing thanks 
 John Wagner
john.wagner@apgecm.com 
 johnwags 
 Author email 
 Nov 7, 2026 
 20 hrs ago 
 0

 Twitter 
 WhatsApp

 Email

 WhatsApp

 Print 
 Copy article link 
 Save 
 Yes, I know Halloween is barely past, and Christmas is on the horizon.
 But the next traditional holiday is one that I feel is both misunderstood and under-appreciated.
 We are only a few weeks away from Thanksgiving. This holiday, which falls on the fourth Thursday in November, is our annual reminder to eat too much before we watch the Lions and Cowboys host football games.
 Wait a second, I may have that wrong.
 Thanksgiving traces its roots to 1621, when English settlers in Plymouth, Massachusetts, shared a harvest feast with members of the Wampanoag people. The gathering took place amid a complicated relationship between the two groups, which included diplomacy and efforts to maintain an alliance. It was a moment in history that has since become part of our national tradition of giving thanks.
 In 1863, then-president Abraham Lincoln proclaimed a national “Thanksgiving Day” in part to foster unity in a splintered country, and Congress formally established the federal holiday in 1941.
 I know that my children groaned when I asked them each Thanksgiving what they were thankful for. My point was to remind them that, even when times seemed difficult, there are people, moments and small acts of kindness that can buoy us.
 The Thanksgiving season also can be a time when we remember people we should thank — but often do not acknowledge. This is a long list that includes police and fire departments, custodians, bus drivers, doctors and nurses, volunteers — even editors who clean up the mistakes and typos of writers.
 Thanks, Boss.
 We can all probably make a list of people we are thankful for, whether it is the teacher who helped us in school, the boss who supported us at work, or the friend or relative who made a difference in our life.
 But is saying “thanks” enough? How often do we say or type the words “thank you” to someone who does something nice for you, without even giving a thought to the gift we are giving? And I do mean “gift,” because a server who notices your empty coffee cup and refills it without being asked, or a store employee who goes the extra mile to make sure you are satisfied with your purchase, is offering something beyond the basic transaction.
 Sometimes I find myself mechanically saying “thank you” without actually thinking about the gift of kindness that someone has shown me. I wonder now if I take for granted those acts of kindness that are showered upon me for no reason — except that someone chose to be thoughtful.
 So this November, I decided to change that. As October ended, I made a list of 30 people I wanted to thank for their kindness to me. I would prefer to not share that list; I’d rather thank these people individually than turn it into a public display. And the truth is, the list is much longer than 30 names.
 My goal is to hand out 30 thank-you cards this month. I know a thank-you card cannot fully express what someone has meant to me, but writing it gives me a chance to reflect on and acknowledge that person’s contribution to my life.
 Perhaps these cards will be only the beginning. I would like to find other ways to turn my gratitude into actions that make someone else’s life a little better.
 Would you join me in this Thanksgiving celebration? You do not have to write 30 cards. Just choose one person in your life and tell them, before Thanksgiving, what they have done that you appreciate and why it matters to you.
 I am grateful we have a day set aside to give thanks, spend time with family, and reflect on our lives. But I want to do more than give thanks on one day. I want the people who have made a difference in my life to know how much I appreciate them.
 It seems ironic that the day after we set aside time to give thanks, we plunge into the unofficial holiday of Black Friday, when the focus shifts to what we want rather than what we already have.
 This year, I know which one of those holidays will get more of my attention.
 John Wagner is the community editor of the County News Review.
